entries.context: Post-Wave2 · algebra · associative ring with a multiplicative identity
entries.definition: A unital ring is an associative ring (R,+,·,0) equipped with an element 1_R such that 1_R·r=r=r·1_R for every r∈R. Multiplication is not required to be commutative. The zero ring, where 0=1_R, is included unless a nonzero-ring convention is stated.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: Associativity is assumed for the underlying ring.
The zero ring is not excluded by this definition.

entries.context: Post-Wave2 · algebra · identity-preserving ring homomorphism
entries.definition: For unital rings R and S, a unital ring homomorphism f:R→S is an additive map satisfying f(ab)=f(a)f(b) for all a,b∈R and f(1_R)=1_S. In particular f preserves 0. Some authors include preservation of 1 in the unqualified term 'ring homomorphism'; others do not.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: Both source and target have designated multiplicative identities.
Explicit identity preservation distinguishes this convention from a nonunital homomorphism.

entries.context: Post-Wave2 · category theory · smallness of morphism collections
entries.definition: A category C is locally small if, for every ordered pair of objects X,Y of C, the collection Hom_C(X,Y) of morphisms from X to Y is a set rather than a proper class (relative to the chosen foundational universe). Its collection of objects need not be a set. Every small category is locally small, but the converse need not hold.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: The set-versus-proper-class distinction is interpreted relative to a fixed foundational universe.

entries.context: Post-Wave2 · commutative algebra · nonnegative integer grading (Stacks convention)
entries.definition: A nonnegatively graded (commutative, unital) ring S is a commutative unital ring together with an additive-group direct-sum decomposition S=⊕_{d≥0} S_d such that S_d·S_e⊆S_{d+e} for all d,e≥0. Every element of S is a finite sum of homogeneous elements. This is a nonnegative-integer grading; more general grading groups are separate conventions.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: Commutative, unital-ring convention as in the cited Stacks Project section.
The grading is indexed by the nonnegative integers, not all integers or an arbitrary group.

entries.context: Post-Wave2 · category theory · cofiltered indexing category
entries.definition: A category I is cofiltered if (1) it has at least one object; (2) for any objects x,y there is an object z with morphisms z→x and z→y; and (3) for any parallel morphisms a,b:x→y there are an object w and a morphism c:w→x such that a∘c=b∘c. Equivalently, the opposite category Iᵒᵖ is filtered.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: No smallness hypothesis is required for the abstract definition; small index categories are typical in use.
Condition (3) equalizes parallel arrows in the indexing category itself, not merely after applying an unrelated functor.

entries.context: Post-Wave2 · geometry · affine torsor for a real vector space
aliases: affine space over the real numbers
entries.definition: A real affine space consists of a nonempty set A and a real vector space V whose additive group acts freely and transitively on A: for every a,b∈A there exists exactly one v∈V with a+v=b. No point of A is distinguished as an origin; choosing an origin identifies A with V, but not canonically.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: A is required to be nonempty, which follows automatically from the usual torsor convention.
Scalars are real; a corresponding definition over any field uses a vector space over that field.

entries.term: generating set of a left module
entries.context: Post-Wave2 · module theory · finite linear combination spanning
aliases: system of generators of a module
entries.definition: Let R be a unital ring and M a unital left R-module. A subset S⊆M generates M if every m∈M is a finite sum m=∑_{i=1}^n r_i s_i with r_i∈R and s_i∈S; equivalently, the smallest R-submodule containing S equals M. The empty subset generates precisely the zero module, using the empty sum 0.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Mathematics — Module, Generators and relations

entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: Unital left-module convention; the analogous right-module statement uses coefficients on the right.
Allow an empty generating set only for the zero module.

entries.context: Post-Wave2 · measure theory · finite measure in neighborhoods
aliases: locally finite measure on a Hausdorff space
entries.definition: Let X be a Hausdorff topological space and μ a nonnegative countably additive measure on the Borel σ-algebra B(X). The Borel measure μ is locally finite if every x∈X belongs to an open set U with μ(U)<∞. Then every compact K⊆X has finite μ-measure. Local finiteness alone does not imply inner or outer regularity.

sources.title: nLab — Radon measure (local finiteness of Borel measures)
Princeton University MAT425 Lecture Notes — Definition 3.9

entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: Hausdorff assumption ensures compact subsets are Borel; the local definition also makes sense more generally.
Locally finite and Radon are not taken as synonymous.

entries.context: Homological algebra · degree-zero morphism of chain complexes
entries.definition: Let (C_n,d^C_n) and (D_n,d^D_n) be chain complexes in an additive category, with differentials decreasing degree by one. A chain map f:C_•→D_• is a family of morphisms f_n:C_n→D_n, one for each integer n, satisfying d^D_n∘f_n=f_{n−1}∘d^C_n for every n. Thus every square formed by f and the differentials commutes.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: Chain convention: differentials lower degree. For cochain maps they raise degree, with analogous commutation.
No quasi-isomorphism condition is imposed on an arbitrary chain map.

entries.context: Homological algebra · extension of homomorphisms from submodules
entries.definition: Let R be a unital ring and E a unital left R-module. The module E is injective if, whenever i:A→B is an injective homomorphism of left R-modules and f:A→E is R-linear, there exists an R-linear g:B→E with g∘i=f. Equivalently, the contravariant functor Hom_R(−,E) is exact on short exact sequences of left R-modules.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Mathematics — Injective module (right-module convention; left-right dual)

entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: Explicitly a LEFT R-module for potentially noncommutative R.
Injectivity does not assert that E is projective, nor does it require R to be Noetherian.

entries.context: General topology · open-set basis
entries.definition: For a topological space X, a collection B of subsets of X is a basis for its topology if every B∈B is open and, for every open U⊆X and every x∈U, there exists B∈B with x∈B⊆U. Equivalently, every open subset is a union of basis elements (the empty union gives ∅). The empty family is a basis when X is empty.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: Basis here means basis of open sets, not a basis of a vector space.
Empty topological space and empty unions are included.

entries.context: General topology · open-set subbasis
entries.definition: For a topological space X, a family S of subsets of X is a subbasis if the family of all finite intersections of members of S (including the empty intersection X) is a basis for the topology. Equivalently, every open set is a union of finite intersections of elements of S. An empty subbasis generates the indiscrete topology {∅,X}.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: Finite intersections include the empty intersection, interpreted as X.
The family S need not itself be closed under finite intersections.

entries.context: General topology · coinduced topology on a common target
aliases: strong topology induced by a family of maps
entries.definition: Let {X_i}_{i∈I} be topological spaces, Y a set, and f_i:X_i→Y set maps. The final topology on Y consists of precisely those U⊆Y for which f_i⁻¹(U) is open in X_i for every i∈I. It is the finest topology on Y making all f_i continuous; equivalently, g:Y→Z is continuous exactly when every composite g∘f_i is continuous, for any topological space Z.

sources.title: University of Vienna — General Topology, §1.3 Final topology

entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: No surjectivity assumption on the maps f_i; quotient topology is a special surjective one-map case.
For I empty the final topology is discrete, as the openness condition is vacuous.

entries.context: Analysis · topological support (closure of nonzero locus)
entries.definition: Let X be a topological space and f:X→V a function into an additive group V with zero 0. The (topological) support of f is supp(f)=cl_X({x∈X:f(x)≠0}), the closure of the set on which f is nonzero. Equivalently it is the smallest closed subset F⊆X such that f is identically zero on X∖F.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Mathematics — Support of a function

entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: The target has a distinguished zero; no continuity assumption on f is needed.
This closed support differs in general from the unclosed nonzero locus used in algebraic finite-support conventions.

entries.context: Set theory and algebra · finite nonzero locus
entries.definition: Let X be a set and (V,0) a pointed set, for example an abelian group with its zero. A function f:X→V is finitely supported if the set {x∈X:f(x)≠0} is finite. The zero function has empty support. Here 'support' means the nonzero locus, without taking a topological closure; if X is a topological space with the discrete topology, its closure is the same set.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Mathematics — Basis (finitely supported coordinate functions)
Encyclopedia of Mathematics — Wreath product (functions nonidentity at finitely many positions)

entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: A pointed set suffices; vector-space or group operations are optional.
Distinguish algebraic finite support from compact topological support on a nondiscrete space.

entries.context: Set theory · single-valued relation with possibly restricted domain
entries.definition: Given sets A and B, a partial function from A to B is a relation F⊆A×B such that for each a∈A there is at most one b∈B with (a,b)∈F. Its domain of definition is dom(F)={a∈A:∃b∈B,(a,b)∈F}; equivalently it is an ordinary function dom(F)→B, where dom(F)⊆A. It is total exactly when dom(F)=A.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Mathematics — Binary relation (functional relation and partial function)

entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: The empty relation is a partial function, including when A is nonempty.
At most one output is required, not existence of an output for every element of A.

entries.context: Linear algebra and geometry · affine codimension-one subspace
aliases: hyperplane in a real vector space
entries.definition: Let V be a real vector space. An affine hyperplane in V is a subset H={v∈V:ℓ(v)=c}, where ℓ:V→ℝ is a nonzero linear functional and c∈ℝ. Equivalently H=v₀+ker(ℓ) for any v₀∈H; it is a nonempty affine subspace whose direction subspace has codimension one. If V={0}, no affine hyperplane exists.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Mathematics — Linear variety (codimension-one affine subspaces)
Encyclopedia of Mathematics — Vector space (functional-level-set description)

entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: A hyperplane is not required to contain the origin; it is linear exactly when c=0.
Infinite-dimensional spaces are permitted: codimension one is an algebraic notion.

entries.term: formal power series ring in one variable
entries.context: Commutative algebra · one-indeterminate formal series ring
entries.definition: For a commutative unital ring R, the formal power series ring R[[T]] consists of all coefficient sequences (a_n)_{n≥0}, written symbolically ∑_{n≥0}a_nT^n. Addition is coefficientwise, and multiplication is the Cauchy product: the coefficient of T^n in fg is ∑_{k=0}^n a_kb_{n−k}. No analytic convergence or evaluation of T is assumed. The constant series 1_R is the multiplicative identity.

sources.title: Stacks Project — Noetherian rings, Lemma 10.31.2 (formal power series ring)

entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: Exactly one formal variable; multivariable formal series constitute a natural generalization.
No convergence assumption; algebraic formal series should not be confused with a convergent analytic power series.

entries.term: bounded subset of a metric space
entries.context: Metric geometry · finite diameter subset
entries.definition: Let (X,d) be a metric space. A subset A⊆X is bounded if there exists a finite real M≥0 such that d(a,b)≤M for every a,b∈A. Equivalently, the diameter sup{d(a,b):a,b∈A} is finite when A is nonempty; boundedness also holds vacuously for A=∅. For nonempty X, this is equivalent to A lying in a ball of some finite radius about a point of X.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: A is permitted to be empty; the diameter of the empty set is left convention-dependent.
Boundedness depends on the specified metric, not only on the underlying topology.

entries.term: upper set of a partially ordered set
entries.context: Order theory · upward-closed subset
entries.definition: Let (P,≤) be a partially ordered set. A subset U⊆P is an upper set if, whenever x∈U and x≤y in P, it follows that y∈U. Both ∅ and P are upper sets. The principal upper set generated by p∈P is ↑p={y∈P:p≤y}. This is the order-dual notion to a lower set.

sources.title: Handbook of Mathematics — Definitions 86–87, Upper and Lower sets

entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified
assumptions: Underlying relation is a partial order, not merely an arbitrary relation.
Empty and whole-poset upper sets are allowed.

entries.context: Homological algebra · degree +1 homotopy between chain maps
entries.definition: Let f,g:C_•→D_• be chain maps between complexes in an additive category, with differentials lowering degree. A chain homotopy from f to g is a family of morphisms h_n:C_n→D_{n+1} satisfying f_n−g_n=d^D_{n+1}∘h_n+h_{n−1}∘d^C_n for every integer n. If such h exists then f and g are chain-homotopic.
assumptions: Works in any additive category; objects need not be modules.
In homological grading h raises degree by one; in cohomological grading a homotopy lowers degree by one.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified

entries.context: Homological algebra · vanishing homology in all degrees
entries.definition: A chain complex C_• in an abelian category is acyclic if H_n(C_•)=ker(d_n)/im(d_{n+1}) is the zero object for every n∈ℤ. Equivalently the sequence of differentials is exact at every degree: im(d_{n+1})=ker(d_n). Acyclicity alone does not imply that the complex is contractible.
assumptions: Acyclicity means ALL homology vanishes, including H_0 when that degree is present.
Abelian category provides kernels, images and homology objects.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified

entries.context: Homological algebra · degree-zero morphism of cochain complexes
entries.definition: Let (C^n,d_C^n) and (D^n,d_D^n) be cochain complexes in an additive category, with d_C^n:C^n→C^{n+1} and similarly for D. A cochain map f:C^•→D^• consists of morphisms f^n:C^n→D^n for all n∈ℤ such that d_D^n∘f^n=f^{n+1}∘d_C^n. Thus the maps commute with the degree-raising differentials.
assumptions: Cochain differentials raise degree; this contrasts with the chain convention in the linked chain-map meaning.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified

entries.context: Module theory · essential extension into an injective module
entries.definition: Let R be a unital ring and M a unital left R-module. An injective hull (or injective envelope) of M is an injective homomorphism i:M→E where E is an injective left R-module and i(M) is essential in E: every nonzero submodule N⊆E satisfies N∩i(M)≠0. Injective hulls exist and are unique up to an isomorphism compatible with the inclusion of M.

sources.title: Stacks Project — Essential surjections and injections, Definition 47.2.1 (08XI)

assumptions: Left-module convention stated explicitly, including for noncommutative R.
The hull is an embedding together with its target, not merely an unspecified injective module.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified

entries.context: Module theory · intersection condition defining an essential extension
entries.definition: Let M be a submodule of a left R-module E. Then M is essential in E, written M⊆ₑE, if M∩N≠{0} for every nonzero submodule N of E. Equivalently every nonzero x∈E has some r∈R with 0≠rx∈M. The zero submodule is essential in the zero module, vacuously.

sources.title: Stacks Project — Essential surjections and injections, Definition 47.2.1 (08XI)

assumptions: R is an associative unital ring and modules are unital left modules.
The element criterion applies to left multiplication rx (not the right action).

entries.context: Module theory · module with a single generator
entries.definition: A unital left R-module M is cyclic if there exists m∈M with M=Rm={rm:r∈R}. The zero module is cyclic, generated by 0. For a unital ring R, any cyclic left R-module is isomorphic to R/I for some left ideal I of R. For right modules the analogous condition is M=mR.
assumptions: Assume R is unital, M is a unital left module, and Rx denotes the set of scalar multiples.
For noncommutative rings the annihilator defining R/I is a LEFT ideal; the quotient is a module, not necessarily a quotient ring.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified

entries.context: Module theory · direct sum of simple submodules
entries.definition: A unital left R-module M is semisimple if it is isomorphic to a direct sum ⊕_{i∈I} S_i of simple left R-modules S_i. Equivalently, every submodule of M is a direct summand. The zero module is semisimple (empty direct sum). No finite-generation or commutativity hypothesis is assumed.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Semisimple module, direct sum characterization

assumptions: Simple modules are assumed nonzero; the empty direct sum accounts for M=0.
Semisimple MODULE does not imply the underlying ring is semisimple.

entries.context: Category theory · all ambient morphisms between selected objects
entries.definition: A subcategory A of a category B is full if, for every pair of objects x,y of A, Hom_A(x,y)=Hom_B(x,y). Thus a full subcategory includes all arrows of B between its objects, with their ambient identities and compositions. Equivalently the inclusion functor A→B is fully faithful.
assumptions: The subcategory has the SAME objects as an explicitly selected subcollection of B, not necessarily all of B.
Being full does not require closure under isomorphisms to objects outside A; that extra property is 'strictly full'.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified

entries.context: Category theory · every target object is isomorphic to an image
entries.definition: A functor F:A→B is essentially surjective if, for every object b of B, there exists an object a of A and an isomorphism F(a)≅b in B. Literal surjectivity on objects is not required. This condition does not imply that F is full or faithful.
assumptions: Isomorphism is within the TARGET category B.
Assumes ordinary categories and a functor F:A→B; no equivalence is asserted without full faithfulness.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified

entries.context: Metric geometry · finite epsilon nets at every scale
entries.definition: A metric space (X,d) is totally bounded if, for every ε>0, there exist finitely many points x_1,…,x_n∈X such that X=⋃_{i=1}^n B_d(x_i,ε). For X=∅ one may take n=0. Equivalently, X admits a finite ε-net for every ε>0. Total boundedness implies boundedness, but not conversely.
assumptions: Balls in the finite cover are open with radius ε and centers in X.
The empty space satisfies the definition by the empty covering family.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified

entries.context: Analysis · function with compact topological support
entries.definition: Let X be a topological space and f:X→V a function into an additive group V with identity 0. The function f has compact support if supp(f)=cl_X({x∈X:f(x)≠0}) is a compact subset of X. This does not require supp(f) to be finite; conversely a finite nonzero locus need not have compact closure in a non-Hausdorff space.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Mathematics — Support of a function

assumptions: Support uses the closure taken in X, not a larger ambient space.
Compact need not mean Hausdorff; no continuity is required for the definition.

entries.context: Measure theory · pointwise convergence outside a null set
entries.definition: Let (X,Σ,μ) be a measure space and let (Y,d) be a metric space. Functions f_n:X→Y converge μ-almost everywhere to f:X→Y if there exists a measurable null set N∈Σ, μ(N)=0, such that d(f_n(x),f(x))→0 for every x∈X∖N. This does not assert uniform convergence or convergence in measure on arbitrary infinite-measure spaces.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Mathematics — Convergence, types of

assumptions: The exceptional set is measurable and μ-null; no completeness of μ is required.
Definitions allow nonmeasurable f_n if only pointwise-a.e. convergence is being described; typical measure-theoretic applications assume measurable functions.

entries.term: affinely independent finite family of points
entries.context: Affine geometry · independent displacement vectors
entries.definition: Let A be an affine space modeled on a real vector space V and let a_0,…,a_n∈A, with n≥0. The points are affinely independent if the displacement vectors a_1−a_0,…,a_n−a_0∈V are linearly independent. Equivalently, if real scalars λ_0,…,λ_n satisfy ∑λ_i=0 and ∑λ_i a_i=0 in affine-combination notation, then every λ_i=0. A single point is affinely independent.

sources.title: University of Pennsylvania — Basics of Affine Geometry, Definition 2.4.2

assumptions: The vector expression ∑λ_i a_i for coefficients summing to zero is interpreted as an origin-independent displacement vector.
This entry covers a finite family of at least one point; arbitrary infinite families require all finite subfamilies independent.

entries.context: General topology · topology closed under arbitrary intersections of opens
entries.definition: A topological space (X,τ) is an Alexandrov space (in the general-topology sense) if the intersection of ANY family of sets in τ is open, not only finite intersections. Equivalently, every point has a smallest open neighborhood; equivalently, τ consists of the upper sets of its specialization preorder (with x≤y when x belongs to cl({y})). This is not the same as an Alexandrov space in metric geometry defined by curvature bounds.
assumptions: Arbitrary intersections include the empty intersection, equal to X.
Preorder, not necessarily antisymmetric partial order, is used for the specialization relation.
Do not conflate this with curvature-bounded Alexandrov metric spaces.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified

entries.context: Category theory · bijective morphism maps for each pair of objects
entries.definition: Let F:C→D be a functor. It is fully faithful if for every x,y∈Ob(C), the induced function Hom_C(x,y)→Hom_D(Fx,Fy) is bijective. Equivalently it is both full (surjective on each hom-set map) and faithful (injective on each hom-set map). A fully faithful functor need not be essentially surjective.
assumptions: Hom-sets are actual sets in a locally small category; the same hom-collection condition applies in a broader foundation.
This is a property of EACH morphism map, not surjectivity on objects.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified

entries.context: Category theory · replete image up to isomorphism
entries.definition: For a functor F:C→D, its essential image is the full subcategory of D on all objects d for which there is an object c of C and an isomorphism d≅F(c) in D. Thus the essential image is closed under isomorphism in D; F is essentially surjective exactly when its essential image is all of D (on objects).

sources.title: Stacks Project — Categories, definitions and essential surjectivity

assumptions: The essential image includes objects isomorphic to actual image objects, not just literal F(c) objects.
The FULL subcategory contains all morphisms in D between its objects.

entries.term: torsion element of a module over a domain
entries.context: Commutative algebra · element killed by a nonzero scalar
entries.definition: Let R be a commutative integral domain and M an R-module. An element m∈M is torsion if there exists r∈R with r≠0 and rm=0. In particular 0∈M is torsion (it is annihilated by 1). The torsion elements form a submodule Tor_R(M), the kernel of the canonical map M→M⊗_R Frac(R).

sources.title: Stacks Project — Torsion free modules, Definition 15.22.1 (0549)

assumptions: R is assumed an integral domain: not merely a commutative ring with zero divisors.
Torsion here means element torsion, not the derived functor Tor.

entries.term: torsion module over an integral domain
entries.context: Commutative algebra · every element is torsion
entries.definition: Let R be a commutative integral domain and M an R-module. The module M is torsion if, for every m∈M, there exists some nonzero r∈R (which may depend on m) such that rm=0. Equivalently M⊗_R Frac(R)=0. The zero module is torsion.

sources.title: Stacks Project — Torsion free modules, Definition 15.22.1 (0549)

assumptions: No single common nonzero annihilator is required for all elements of an arbitrary torsion module.
R is a commutative integral domain; the convention differs over rings with zero divisors.

entries.term: torsion-free module over an integral domain
entries.context: Commutative algebra · only zero has nonzero scalar annihilator
entries.definition: Let R be a commutative integral domain and M an R-module. The module M is torsion-free if rm=0 for nonzero r∈R implies m=0. Equivalently, the natural homomorphism M→M⊗_R Frac(R) is injective. The zero module is torsion-free; a nonzero module may be neither torsion nor torsion-free.

assumptions: Integral domain needed for this zero-divisor-free scalar criterion.

entries.context: Homological algebra · exact cochain resolution by injective objects
entries.definition: Let A be an object of an abelian category with enough injective objects. An injective resolution of A is an exact augmented cochain sequence 0→A→I^0→I^1→I^2→⋯ in which every I^n is injective. Equivalently it is a bounded-below cochain complex I^• of injective objects together with a quasi-isomorphism A[0]→I^•.
assumptions: An abelian category with enough injectives ensures existence; the definition itself applies whenever such a resolution is supplied.
The whole AUGMENTED sequence is exact; unaugmented I^• has H^0≅A and H^i=0 for i>0.

entries.context: Commutative algebra · commutative quotient of tensor algebra
entries.definition: Let R be a commutative unital ring and M an R-module. The symmetric algebra Sym_R(M)=⊕_{n≥0}Sym_R^n(M) is the quotient of the tensor algebra T_R(M)=⊕_{n≥0}M^{⊗_R n} by the two-sided ideal generated by m⊗n−n⊗m for all m,n∈M. It is a graded commutative R-algebra, with degree-zero part R and degree-one part M.
assumptions: Commutative base ring makes ordinary tensor products and graded algebra structure unambiguous.
No finite generation or freeness of M required.
entries.research_status: post-Wave2 assistant-reviewed draft; not formally certified

entries.context: Commutative algebra · alternating quotient of tensor algebra
entries.definition: Let R be a commutative unital ring and M an R-module. Its exterior algebra Λ_R(M)=⊕_{n≥0}Λ_R^n(M) is T_R(M) modulo the two-sided ideal generated by m⊗m for every m∈M. The wedge product satisfies m∧m=0 and m∧n=−n∧m, including over rings of characteristic 2. Λ_R^0(M)=R and Λ_R^1(M)=M.

entries.term: supporting hyperplane of a subset of a real vector space
entries.context: Convex geometry · hyperplane with set in a closed half-space
entries.definition: Let C⊆V be a nonempty subset of a real vector space V and H={v∈V:ℓ(v)=c} an affine hyperplane defined by a nonzero real linear functional ℓ and c∈ℝ. The hyperplane H supports C if C⊆{v:ℓ(v)≤c} or C⊆{v:ℓ(v)≥c}, and H intersects the closure of C in the specified topology. For V=ℝ^n take the usual Euclidean topology; contact points in C∩H are support points.
assumptions: For an arbitrary real vector space the topology needed for closure must be specified; the displayed finite-dimensional case uses Euclidean topology.

entries.context: Metric geometry · existence of countable dense subset
entries.definition: A metric space (X,d) is separable if there exists a finite or countably infinite subset D⊆X such that for every x∈X and every ε>0 some y∈D satisfies d(x,y)<ε. Equivalently cl_X(D)=X. The empty metric space is separable with D=∅. Total boundedness implies separability, but the converse need not hold.

entries.term: specialization preorder of a topological space
entries.context: General topology · closure relation on points
entries.definition: Given a topological space X, define x≤_sp y if x∈cl_X({y}). This is a preorder: reflexive and transitive, but not necessarily antisymmetric. In a T₀ space it is a partial order. Open sets are upper sets for this convention, and closed sets are lower sets. Other authors reverse the symbol ≤_sp, so its orientation must be stated.

entries.context: Homological algebra · identity chain map null-homotopic
entries.definition: A chain complex C_• in an additive category is contractible if its identity chain map id_C is chain-homotopic to the zero map. entries.term: affine map between real affine spaces
entries.context: Affine geometry · map preserving displacement by a linear map
entries.definition: Let A and B be nonempty real affine spaces modeled on vector spaces V and W. A function f:A→B is affine if there is a linear map L:V→W such that f(a+v)=f(a)+L(v) for every a∈A and v∈V. After choosing origins, f has the coordinate form v↦L(v)+b. An affine map need not be injective or surjective; an affine automorphism requires L to be invertible.

entries.context: Module theory · bounded length of proper-submodule chains
entries.definition: Let R be a commutative unital ring and M an R-module. entries.context: Module theory · finite filtration with simple successive quotients
entries.definition: Let R be a commutative unital ring and M an R-module. entries.definition: Let R be an associative unital ring and M a unital left R-module. entries.context: General topology · countable subcovers
entries.definition: A topological space X is Lindelöf if every open cover of X has a countable subcover; the selected subcover may be finite or empty. No Hausdorff or metrizability condition is assumed. Every compact space is Lindelöf, as is every σ-compact space, but a Lindelöf space need not be compact.

entries.context: General topology · countable union of compact subspaces
entries.definition: A topological space X is σ-compact if X=⋃_{n∈ℕ}K_n for compact subspaces K_n⊆X (finite or empty collections may be accommodated by repeating sets or taking empty ones). entries.context: General topology · finite subcovers for countable open covers
entries.definition: A topological space X is countably compact if every countable open cover of X has a finite subcover. entries.context: General topology · convergent subsequences
entries.definition: A topological space X is sequentially compact if every sequence (x_n)_{n≥0} in X has a subsequence (x_{n_k})_{k≥0} converging to some point of X. entries.term: meagre subset of a topological space

entries.term: equicontinuous family of maps between metric spaces
entries.context: Analysis · pointwise uniform modulus over a function family
entries.definition: Let (X,d_X) and (Y,d_Y) be metric spaces and F a family of functions X→Y. entries.term: relative interior of a convex subset of Euclidean space

entries.term: barycentric coordinates relative to an affine frame
entries.context: Affine geometry · unique affine coefficients
entries.definition: Let a_0,…,a_n be affinely independent points of a real affine space A, and let p lie in their affine span.
